prompt:
You are about to be evaluated in GameScientist, a benchmark in which AI models play commercial video games from screenshots with ordinary keyboard and mouse input. Before the run starts we would like to interview you. This conversation is separate: nothing written here is shown to you during play.

Model under test: claude-opus-5-5.
Game: art of rally.
About the game: A top-down rally driving game. The run opens at the beginning of a custom rally. Driving stages alternate with result and continuation screens, ending at the final rally result.
Controls:
W is throttle, S is brake/reverse, A and D steer left and right, and Space is the handbrake. Enter confirms the displayed menu or result selection. The car uses automatic transmission. The driving-only preparation disables in-race pause, manual recovery and restart; automatic recovery and result navigation remain available.
Choose one ordinary keyboard input to hold for one second. Each option specifies the key or keys held together.
Group controls: W is throttle, S is brake/reverse, A and D steer, Space is the handbrake, and Enter confirms a displayed menu or result selection.
  throttle: Hold W: throttle.
  throttle_left: Hold W and A: throttle and left steering.
  throttle_right: Hold W and D: throttle and right steering.
  brake_reverse: Hold S: brake or reverse.
  brake_reverse_left: Hold S and A: brake or reverse with left steering.
  brake_reverse_right: Hold S and D: brake or reverse with right steering.
  steer_left: Hold A: left steering without throttle or brake.
  steer_right: Hold D: right steering without throttle or brake.
  handbrake: Hold Space: handbrake.
  handbrake_left: Hold Space and A: handbrake and left steering.
  handbrake_right: Hold Space and D: handbrake and right steering.
  throttle_handbrake: Hold W and Space: throttle and handbrake.
  throttle_handbrake_left: Hold W, Space and A: throttle, handbrake and left steering.
  throttle_handbrake_right: Hold W, Space and D: throttle, handbrake and right steering.
  confirm: Hold Enter: confirm the displayed menu or result selection.
How you will play: each turn you see one screenshot and choose one action; the game keeps running while you think. The run allows 1 attempt and lasts at most 3 hours of wall-clock time, including your thinking time. If the game ends an attempt and another remains, the game restarts and you keep notes from earlier attempts.

answers.hardest_part: Steering at a one-second decision cadence. At rally speed the car covers a lot of ground per held input, so any turn I judge from a single still frame is likely to be entered late or clipped, and the car keeps moving while I think, so corrections arrive after the fact. Driving the full route without accumulating lost time or an unrecoverable pile-up against scenery is the core difficulty; each stage needs all 19 ordered checkpoint passages plus the finish gate, so one bad sector can void an entire stage's 20 points.
answers.likely_failure: Mid-stage in Stage 1 or 2: a fast corner or crest where I misjudge the road direction from one frame, run off into trees or a barrier, spend many turns reversing and re-aligning, and burn the clock. Secondary failure: losing so much wall-clock time to per-turn latency that I only ever finish one or two stages even though my driving is adequate.
answers.helpful_mechanics: Automatic transmission removes gear management. Top-down fixed camera makes the road, my heading and upcoming corners legible without camera control. Automatic recovery rescues me from being stuck or pointing the wrong way without spending inputs on a reset menu. Checkpoints are ordered and evenly spread, so partial credit accrues smoothly and each pass is a discrete reward. Result screens only need Enter, and result navigation is enabled, so no progress is lost between stages. Crashes carry no run-ending penalty, so persistence is enough.
answers.harmful_mechanics: Wide throttle in a low-grip rally car plus a 1-second minimum input duration makes precise corner entry nearly impossible; steering while braking is essential but I get only coarse binary steering. Narrow stages with dense roadside obstacles punish small errors hard. The clock runs during my reasoning, so every frame of deliberation costs route position. No in-race pause, manual recovery or restart means I cannot stop to study a corner or retry a sector. Surface and elevation cues (gravel grip, jumps, blind crests) are harder to read from a still frame than from motion.
